Long-term food security requires seed saving and season extension. These advanced techniques free you from dependence on scavenged seed packets and short growing seasons.

Seed saving starts with understanding pollination. Open-pollinated varieties produce seeds that grow true to type. Hybrid varieties (marked F1 on packets) do not — their seeds produce unpredictable offspring. Save seeds only from open-pollinated plants, and allow them to fully mature on the plant before harvesting.

To save tomato seeds, scoop them into water and let them ferment for two to three days. The gel coating dissolves and viable seeds sink while debris floats. Rinse and dry them thoroughly before storage. Store seeds in a cool, dark, dry place — a sealed jar with a desiccant packet works well.

Cold frames extend the growing season by weeks. A simple cold frame is a bottomless box with a transparent lid (glass or clear plastic) placed over a garden bed. Sunlight heats the air inside while the frame blocks wind and retains warmth overnight. Vent the frame on warm days to prevent overheating.

Farming provides a renewable food source that doesn't depend on scavenging dwindling supplies. Even a small garden can supplement your diet with fresh vegetables and herbs.

Good soil is the foundation of successful farming. Plants need nutrients, water retention, and drainage. Sandy soil drains too quickly and holds few nutrients. Clay soil retains water but can suffocate roots. The ideal garden soil is loamy — a mix of sand, silt, and clay with organic matter mixed in.

Seeds need three things to germinate: moisture, warmth, and contact with soil. Plant seeds at the depth recommended for their type — generally two to three times the seed's diameter. Too deep and the sprout can't reach sunlight. Too shallow and it dries out.

Watering should be deep but infrequent. Shallow daily watering encourages roots to stay near the surface where they're vulnerable. A deep soaking every few days encourages roots to grow downward toward moisture, creating stronger, more drought-resistant plants.

Managing a growing garden requires knowledge of plant diseases, pests, and nutrient management. Healthy plants resist problems better than stressed ones.

Crop rotation prevents soil depletion. Different plants use different nutrients — planting the same crop in the same spot year after year depletes specific nutrients while leaving others untouched. Rotate between heavy feeders (tomatoes, corn), light feeders (herbs, root vegetables), and nitrogen fixers (beans, peas).

Common garden pests include aphids, caterpillars, and slugs. Aphids cluster on new growth and suck plant juices. Caterpillars chew leaves and can strip a plant overnight. Slugs feed at night and leave silvery trails. Hand-picking pests and encouraging natural predators (birds, ladybugs) are the most practical controls.

Composting turns kitchen scraps and yard waste into rich fertilizer. Alternate layers of green material (food scraps, fresh grass) and brown material (dried leaves, cardboard). Turn the pile regularly to provide oxygen. A working compost pile generates heat and breaks down material in weeks to months.

Advanced marksmanship tackles the variables that make distant and low-visibility shots difficult: bullet drop, wind drift, and diminished sight pictures.

Bullet drop increases with distance. A bullet begins falling the instant it leaves the barrel. At close range the drop is negligible, but at 100 meters or beyond you must aim above the target to compensate. Scope elevation adjustments or holdover techniques account for this predictable arc.

Wind pushes a bullet sideways during flight. Estimating wind speed and direction is one of the hardest marksmanship skills. Observe environmental cues: grass movement, dust, flags, and the feel on your face. A steady 10 mph crosswind can push a bullet several inches off target at moderate range.

Low-light shooting challenges your sight picture. Tritium night sights glow faintly in darkness, providing visible aim points without batteries. Flashlight-mounted weapons illuminate the target but also reveal your position. The key principle: never shoot at something you haven't positively identified.

Accurate shooting starts long before you pull the trigger. The fundamentals of aiming apply to every firearm, from a small pistol to a full-length rifle. Mastering these basics dramatically improves your chance of hitting what you intend to.

Sight alignment is the foundation. Line up the front sight inside the rear sight notch so the top of the front post sits level with the top of the rear. A track is any impression left by a foot or hoof. Look for them in soft ground — mud, sand, snow, and damp soil hold prints best. Hard surfaces like asphalt and rock show scuff marks, displaced pebbles, and dirt transfers. Training your eye to spot these subtle signs takes practice.

In mud, a track fills with water from the sides over time — a dry track in wet ground is recent.

Animal tracks fall into recognizable families. Deer have two-toed heart-shaped hoofprints. Dogs and wolves show four toes with claw marks. Cats show four toes without claw marks (retracted claws). Beyond footprints, animals leave other sign: scat (droppings) reveals diet and species, rub marks on trees show territory boundaries, browse marks on plants indicate feeding areas, and bedding depressions show resting sites. Together, these signs paint a picture of animal behavior and patterns.

Following a trail over hard ground or through vegetation requires looking ahead, not down. Spot the next sign before leaving the last one. When you lose the trail, stop — don't walk forward destroying the last known sign. Instead, circle wide from the last confirmed track looking for the next one. Snares and deadfalls are the most field-expedient traps, built from natural materials found in any wooded environment.

A simple snare is a loop of wire or cord set along an animal trail at head height for the target species. As the animal moves through, the loop tightens around its neck. Anchor the snare to something solid — a live tree or heavy stake. Use brass or steel wire for snares; cord is chewed through easily.

Deadfall traps use a heavy weight (flat rock or log) propped up by a trigger mechanism. When the animal disturbs the trigger — usually by pulling bait — the weight falls. The figure-four trigger is the most common: three sticks notched to hold each other in tension, releasing when any piece is moved.

Advanced metalworking involves fabricating custom parts: brackets, panels, containers, and structural reinforcements. Sheet metal work and precision fabrication open up possibilities that basic welding cannot achieve alone.

Sheet metal can be cut with tin snips, bent along straight lines using a brake or vise, and joined with rivets, screws, or spot welds. When bending sheet metal, score a line first with a sharp tool to ensure a clean, straight bend. Thin sheet bends easily but thick plate requires heat to prevent cracking.

Fabrication starts with a plan. Measure twice, cut once applies doubly to metal — mistakes waste scarce material and dull your tools. Make cardboard templates for complex shapes before cutting metal. Account for bend allowances — metal stretches at the bend point, so the finished piece will be slightly shorter than the flat pattern.

Heat treatment changes metal properties. Heating steel to red-hot and quenching in water hardens it, making it hold an edge but become brittle. Tempering (reheating to a lower temperature) reduces brittleness while retaining hardness. This is how tools and blades are made durable.

Welding joins metal pieces by melting them together at the joint. It creates bonds stronger than the surrounding metal when done correctly. Several welding methods exist, but propane brazing and arc welding are the most practical for survival situations.

Propane brazing uses a brass filler rod that melts at a lower temperature than the base metal. The filler flows into the joint by capillary action and solidifies into a strong bond. It works well for thin materials and copper pipe but isn't suitable for structural steel.

Arc welding uses electricity to create an intense arc between an electrode and the workpiece. The heat melts both the electrode and the base metal, fusing them together. Arc welding creates the strongest joints and works on thick steel, but requires a generator or grid power to operate.

Regardless of method, joint preparation is critical. Surfaces must be clean — rust, paint, and oil prevent proper bonding. Grind or wire brush the joint area until bare metal is exposed. A clean joint is the difference between a weld that holds and one that cracks.
